recap_md: Nick Carraway, our narrator, recalls his father's advice to reserve judgment of others, though he admits his tolerance has limits. Restless after WWI, he moved East to learn the bond business and rents a small house in West Egg, Long Island, across the bay from the wealthier East Egg. He introduces his old college acquaintance Tom Buchanan, a former football star, and is about to visit Tom and his wife (Nick's cousin) Daisy at their East Egg mansion.

Nick, restless after the war, has settled in West Egg to learn the bond business and gone to visit his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom Buchanan, a wealthy former football star, at their East Egg mansion. Inside he finds Daisy and her friend Jordan Baker lounging on a couch; over drinks the group trades gossip, and Jordan casually mentions Nick's neighbor Gatsby, surprising Daisy. Before dinner Tom launches into a bigoted rant defending a pseudo-scientific book on race, and Jordan quietly tells Nick that Tom has a woman in New York.

Nick has settled in West Egg for the bond business and visited his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom at their East Egg mansion, where a strained dinner - interrupted by a call from Tom's mistress - revealed cracks in the marriage. Daisy, disillusioned, said she hopes her daughter grows up to be 'a beautiful little fool.' Driving home, Nick glimpsed his mysterious neighbor Gatsby standing alone, reaching toward a green light across the water. He now describes the desolate valley of ashes, watched over by the fading eyes of a billboard for Doctor T. J. Eckleburg - the place where, he reveals, he first met Tom's mistress.

Nick, now settled in West Egg, has met his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom at their East Egg mansion, sensed trouble in their marriage, and glimpsed his enigmatic neighbor Gatsby from afar. Tom now pulls Nick off a train at the grim valley of ashes to introduce him to George Wilson's garage - and, in an aside to Wilson, arranges to meet Wilson's wife Myrtle. Myrtle joins Tom and Nick on a trip into New York, buying a puppy along the way, and at her small apartment Tom and Myrtle slip off together while Nick gets thoroughly drunk as Myrtle's sister Catherine and the McKees from downstairs arrive for an increasingly garish party.

At Myrtle's tawdry New York party, gossip swirls about Gatsby's mysterious origins while Myrtle reveals she married the unglamorous George Wilson by mistake and has been having an affair with Tom for years. When Myrtle taunts Tom by shouting Daisy's name, he breaks her nose with a single blow, and the drunken evening ends with Nick dazed at Pennsylvania Station. Nick then turns to his wealthy West Egg neighbor: every weekend, Gatsby's mansion erupts into lavish parties, with orchestras, motorboats, and crowds of guests arriving uninvited.

Unlike most of Gatsby's party guests, Nick receives an actual invitation, and at the party he finds Jordan Baker amid guests trading wild rumors that Gatsby once killed a man or spied for Germany. In the library, a drunk 'owl-eyed' man marvels that Gatsby's books are real, not just decorative props. Then, in a quiet twist, Nick realizes the stranger he's been chatting with all evening is Gatsby himself, who reveals his identity with a rare, reassuring smile.

As the party winds down, Jordan doubts Gatsby's claim to be an Oxford man, and is pulled aside for a private word by his butler. Amid a drunken singer and quarreling couples, Jordan and Gatsby re-emerge together, and Gatsby reminds Nick of a planned hydroplane ride. Leaving, Nick passes a car wrecked in a ditch, its drunk driver insisting someone else was at the wheel - and looking back one last time, sees Gatsby standing alone on his porch, waving a strangely formal goodbye.

Nick explains that Gatsby's parties were only a small part of a summer mostly spent working and wandering New York at night. He grows fond of Jordan Baker despite recognizing she is 'incurably dishonest' - from a lied-about borrowed car to a golf tournament cheating scandal - and admits, half-ironically, to being one of the few honest people he knows. Guests keep speculating that Gatsby is a bootlegger, and Nick recalls the summer's endless parade of party guests, including the permanent fixture Klipspringer. One July morning Gatsby drives over in his conspicuous yellow car to invite Nick to lunch, though Nick's early sense of Gatsby's importance has begun to fade.

During the drive into the city, Gatsby volunteers his life story to Nick: a wealthy Midwestern family (all now dead), an Oxford education, and a period living like a 'young rajah' collecting jewels across Europe, followed by an account of wartime heroism backed by a medal and an Oxford photo. He mentions he'll make a big request of Nick, to be explained by Jordan over tea, and after a traffic stop is smoothed over with a mysterious card, they cross into Manhattan for lunch with Gatsby's business associate Meyer Wolfshiem, who tells a gruesome gangland murder story and repeatedly, admiringly calls Gatsby an 'Oggsford man.'

Wolfshiem, revealed as the man who fixed the 1919 World Series, departs, and Nick unexpectedly runs into Tom, who is introduced to Gatsby - who then quickly disappears. That afternoon Jordan finally tells Nick the real story: in 1917 Louisville, eighteen-year-old Daisy Fay was courted by a young lieutenant named Jay Gatsby before her family kept them apart; drunk the night before her wedding to Tom, she nearly called it off, clutching a letter she wouldn't give up. Jordan traces Daisy and Tom's marriage through his early infidelity and their years abroad, ending with Daisy's strange reaction on hearing Gatsby's name again recently. The real reason for Gatsby's mansion, Jordan reveals, is to be near Daisy across the bay - and his true request is for Nick to invite her to tea.

Gatsby arranges through Nick to have Daisy over for tea, awkwardly offering (and being refused) a vague business connection in return. On the appointed rainy day, Gatsby has Nick's lawn mowed and the house filled with flowers, waiting pale and anxious for her arrival. Their reunion is achingly strained - Gatsby nearly knocks over a clock, then panics and pulls Nick aside insisting the whole visit is a mistake. Left waiting outside in the rain, Nick returns to find Daisy in tears and Gatsby utterly transformed, glowing with sudden happiness.

Relieved the rain has passed, Gatsby tours Nick and Daisy through his opulent mansion, offering a vague, contradictory account of his fortune. Upstairs, faced with his own imported shirts, his joy curdles into restlessness and Daisy bursts into tears at their beauty. Gatsby tells Daisy about the green light on her dock, sensing its symbolic power has faded now that she's actually near - and Nick, sensing a doubt creeping into Gatsby's happiness that reality could never match years of dreaming, quietly leaves the two alone. Nick then reveals what a young reporter's visit implied: Gatsby was really born James Gatz, a poor farm boy who invented 'Jay Gatsby' as his ideal self.

Nick recounts Gatsby's real origin: as a young drifter on Lake Superior, James Gatz filled his nights with grandiose fantasies until Dan Cody's yacht anchored nearby and changed his fate. Gatsby spent five years in Cody's service, but after Cody's death was cheated out of his promised inheritance, left with only manners and polish. Nick then recalls an awkward afternoon when Tom Buchanan rode over uninvited with acquaintances for drinks, one of whom impulsively invited Gatsby to supper before the group maneuvered away without him. Later, Tom accompanies Daisy to one of Gatsby's parties, and Nick senses a new, unfamiliar oppressiveness as Gatsby shows off for her.

At the party, Daisy admits the raw vitality of West Egg appalls her, and afterward Gatsby confides that she didn't enjoy it - insisting, with unwavering conviction, that she must renounce Tom completely, since he believes the past can simply be repeated. Nick recalls Gatsby's memory of the autumn night five years earlier when he first kissed Daisy in Louisville and bound his entire future to her. Gatsby's parties abruptly stop, and he replaces his household staff with people who won't gossip about Daisy's frequent visits. On the summer's hottest day, Nick and Gatsby take a stifling train to the Buchanans', arriving to find Daisy and Jordan lying motionless on a couch in a shaded, cooled room.

Back at the Buchanans', Daisy - emboldened - openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love for him in front of everyone, and over a tense lunch Tom finally realizes, with astonishment, that his wife loves Gatsby. As the group splits into two cars for a trip to New York, Gatsby tells Nick that Daisy's voice is 'full of money'; in the car, an increasingly suspicious Tom interrogates Nick and Jordan and mocks Gatsby's Oxford claim. Stopping for gas, they find George Wilson sick and desperate, having just discovered his wife Myrtle's secret life and wanting to move them both out West - while Myrtle watches jealously from a window, mistaking Jordan for Tom's wife.

Panicked at the thought of losing both wife and mistress, Tom chases down Daisy's car, and the group reconvenes in a stifling suite at the Plaza Hotel. There, under mounting pressure, Gatsby demands that Tom leave Daisy alone and finally admits he truly did study at Oxford - briefly, through a postwar army program. Tom, in turn, delivers a bigoted tirade and demands to know what Gatsby is after; Gatsby answers by declaring that Daisy never loved Tom at all, only him, claiming they've secretly loved each other for five years. Pressed by both men, Daisy reluctantly agrees she never loved Tom - but when Tom forces her to recall specific shared memories, she breaks down and admits she loved Gatsby once, but loved Tom too, shattering Gatsby's belief that she loved no one else.

Having exposed Gatsby's illegal liquor-selling business, Tom - confident the affair is over - sends a devastated Daisy home with Gatsby. Driving back, Nick, realizing it's his thirtieth birthday, reflects unhappily on the years ahead. They soon learn tragedy has struck: George Wilson's wife Myrtle broke free after being locked up and was struck and killed instantly by a car that didn't stop - a big, new, yellow one, according to witnesses. Arriving at the scene, Tom quietly lies to the shattered Wilson, denying it was his own car, then breaks down sobbing over Myrtle once out of the crowd's sight.

Outside the Buchanans' house, a shaken Gatsby reveals to Nick the real truth of the accident: it was Daisy, not himself, who was driving the car that killed Myrtle - and he intends to take the blame to protect her. Peering in a window, Nick sees Tom and Daisy sitting together intimately, like conspirators, and leaves Gatsby standing watch alone outside in the moonlight. Unable to sleep, Nick visits Gatsby again before dawn; nothing happened with Daisy the night before, and Gatsby refuses to leave town until he learns what she will do. Gatsby then recalls falling for Daisy years earlier in wartime Louisville, letting her believe he could give her the life she was used to, before they slept together one October night.

Gatsby recalls holding Daisy in silence by the fire on his last afternoon before shipping overseas; delayed returning from the war, he lost her to Tom, who arrived and won her that spring. At dawn, Gatsby still insists Daisy never truly loved Tom, calling their marriage 'just personal.' Over a subdued breakfast Gatsby asks that his unused pool not be drained, and as Nick leaves for work he shouts to Gatsby that he's worth more than the whole 'rotten crowd' - the only compliment Nick ever pays him. At the office, a cold, final call from Jordan ends their relationship. Nick then backtracks to the night before at the garage: Wilson, rocking in grief for hours, eventually blurts that Myrtle once came home bruised, and when Michaelis finds a hidden dog leash, Wilson takes it as proof of a lover and mutters, 'he killed her.'

As dawn breaks, the grief-stricken Wilson becomes convinced 'he murdered her,' mistaking the fading eyes of a billboard advertisement for the eyes of God watching him. He then wanders on foot for hours, tracked through several towns, arriving in West Egg that afternoon already knowing Gatsby's name. While Gatsby waits by his pool for a phone call that never comes, Wilson shoots him dead before turning the gun on himself. In the chaos that follows, Nick learns that Tom and Daisy have already fled town with their bags, leaving no forwarding address, and his attempts to reach Gatsby's mysterious associate Wolfshiem go nowhere - even a caller with news for Gatsby falls silent on learning he is dead.

Gatsby's death draws almost no one who mattered to him in life: Klipspringer calls only to ask about a pair of shoes he left behind, and Meyer Wolfshiem, though he reminisces fondly about 'making' Gatsby, refuses to attend the funeral, saying he makes a point of staying out of things once a man is dead. Only Gatsby's father, Henry Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, proud that his son belonged among the wealthy East - he shows Nick a boyhood copy of Hopalong Cassidy filled with earnest self-improvement resolutions. As the funeral hour arrives, no other guests come at all; only a small, rain-soaked procession attends the burial, joined unexpectedly by the drunken 'owl-eyed' man from the library, who calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.'

In the story's final movement, Nick - reflecting on his own Christmas homecomings - concludes this has been a story of Westerners unsuited to life in the East, and decides to move back home. He has a last, cold conversation with Jordan Baker, now engaged to someone else, who accuses him of having thrown her over; and a chance meeting with Tom on Fifth Avenue reveals, without remorse, that Tom was the one who told Wilson that Gatsby owned the fatal car. On his last night at West Egg, Nick imagines the island as the first Dutch sailors once saw it, and reflects on Gatsby's doomed dream of recapturing the past - closing with the novel's famous final line about boats borne ceaselessly against the current.
